goal_text: Write a PRD for my side project

nodes.title: What a solo-builder PRD is actually for
nodes.one_liner: Why write one when building alone, and what to leave out

nodes.title: Frame the problem and the 'why'
nodes.one_liner: Capturing the problem, user, and reason to build it

nodes.title: Define scope: what's in, what's out
nodes.one_liner: Drawing MVP boundaries and an explicit non-goals list

nodes.title: Write requirements that guide coding
nodes.one_liner: Turning features into buildable, unambiguous specs

nodes.title: Sketch user flows and screens
nodes.one_liner: Mapping how a user moves through the product

nodes.title: Note technical decisions and constraints
nodes.one_liner: Stack, data model, and dependencies worth pinning down

nodes.title: Pick a few success signals
nodes.one_liner: Lightweight ways to know a feature works

nodes.title: How detailed is detailed enough?
nodes.one_liner: Right depth per section to stay unblocked, not overplan

outline.rationale: The user wants the practical anatomy of a PRD for guiding their own solo build, and is comfortable with their project idea itself. I open with a node reframing the PRD's purpose specifically for a solo context (justifying what to skip), then walk the core document sections in build-dependency order: problem framing, scope/non-goals, requirements, user flows, and technical constraints. I include a deliberately lightweight 'success signals' node rather than a heavy metrics framework, per the deprioritization of collaboration/metrics-heavy content. I deliberately excluded approval workflows, stakeholder alignment, and product-definition help. The final node addresses the user's stated concern about 'how detailed each needs to be' — a distinct, high-value question for a solo builder wary of overplanning. Sections are MECE: purpose, why, scope, requirements, flows, tech, metrics, and calibration each answer a non-overlapping question.
